title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet

epigraph.quote: Cash provided by operating activities in 2025 totaled $5,120 million, or 122% of net earnings, up $1 billion compared to 2024.
epigraph.author: General Dynamics Corporation, FY2025 Form 10-K & Earnings Release (January 2026)

web_blocks.title: 10-Year Financial Ledger & ROIC vs. WACC Spread

web_blocks.html: A ten-year review of General Dynamics (FY2016–FY2025, plus 9M 2026) shows a remarkably steady compounder [1][3][9]. The company absorbed the 2018 CSRA acquisition, navigated the 2020–2021 aviation downturn, and funded heavy shipyard capex. Even so, revenue expanded from $30.56 billion in 2016 to $52.55 billion in 2025 [1][9]. That represents a 6.2% nine-year CAGR, accelerating to 10.1% in 2025 and 10.4% in 9M 2026 [1][3]. Over the same decade, diluted EPS climbed from $9.52 in 2016 to $15.45 in 2025 [9]. Trailing twelve-month EPS reached $17.01 through Q3 2026 [2].

web_blocks.caption: 10-Year Financial Forensics: P&L, Cash Flow & Leverage (FY2016–FY2025)
web_blocks.takeaway: Note: Audited FY2023 Operating Earnings are $4,245M ($4.25B) and Net Earnings are $3,315M ($3.32B), reconciling $12.02 diluted EPS to ~275.8M diluted shares [1][9]. FY2025 Capex is $1,194M per the 2025 Form 10-K ($3,926M FCF); some aggregators report $1,161M ($3,959M FCF) due to software and lease classification [1][5][9].

web_blocks.html: ROIC vs. WACC & Balance Sheet Deleveraging: General Dynamics posts a trailing 13.22% ROIC and 18.01% ROE. Both sit comfortably above an estimated ~7.5%–8.0% WACC for a defense prime, confirming durable value creation. ROE moderated from ~25%–27% in 2016–2019 to ~17%–18% in 2023–2025 as management retained equity to pay down CSRA-era debt [1][9]. Long-term debt fell from $11.40 billion in 2018 to $7.01 billion at year-end 2025. It dropped further to $6,260 million at October 4, 2026 after repaying $1,000 million of notes in June and August 2026 ($500 million each) with cash on hand (Note H) [1][9]. By October 4, 2026, total debt stood at $7,016 million ($756 million current) against $4,388 million in cash and $27,292 million in equity. That cut net debt to $2,628 million (~0.4x EBITDA).

web_blocks.title: Working Capital, Unbilled Receivables & Footnote Forensics

web_blocks.html: Working Capital & Unbilled Receivables Forensics: Working-capital absorption remains a primary forensic watchpoint. At October 4, 2026, current assets held $2,529 million in billed receivables (vs. $2,406M at YE25). Net unbilled receivables reached $8,906 million ($47,157M gross unbilled revenue less $38,251M advances/billings, up from $8,380M at YE25). Inventories stood at $9,124 million, down from $9,232M at year-end (Q3 2026 Form 10-Q, Notes E and F) [1]. Note E flags $1.2 billion in net unbilled receivables on one international tracked-vehicle contract in Combat Systems (down slightly from $1.3 billion at YE25) [1]. Note B explicitly warns that variable consideration realized on that contract could fall below current estimates and materially affect operating results [1]. Offsetting those receivables, customer advances and deposits rose to $11,083 million current plus $2,622 million noncurrent ($13,705 million total). Neither the FY2025 Form 10-K nor the Q3 2026 Form 10-Q discloses any active receivable-factoring (MARPA) facility. That confirms GD's $5,745 million 9M 2026 CFO ($4,827 million FCF; 139% Q3 CFO-to-net-earnings) reflects organic milestone cash collection [1][2].

Goodwill, Debt Maturities, Leases & Pension Forensics: Four off-headline balance-sheet footnotes deserve close scrutiny. First, total goodwill stands at $20,849 million at October 4, 2026 (76.4% of $27,292 million equity). Of that total, $14,515 million (69.6%) sits in Technologies, already net of $1.8 billion in prior impairment losses. Technologies goodwill was last quantitatively tested in Q4 2022 with ~25% fair-value headroom (Q3 2026 10-Q Note G; FY2025 10-K Note A). Second, fixed-rate debt maturities cluster in 2027–2028: $750 million (3.500%) in April 2027, $500 million (2.625%) in November 2027, and $1,000 million (3.750%) in May 2028. That equals $2,250 million over 19 months, alongside a $4 billion committed bank credit facility expiring March 2027 (Note H). Third, total balance-sheet lease liabilities stand at $2,014 million ($334M current + $1,680M noncurrent, Note I). Fourth, underfunded defined-benefit pension plans carried an $11,540 million PBO against $10,606 million plan assets at YE25 (FY2025 10-K, Note S). GD contributed $500 million in cash during Q3 2026 (Note O), cutting noncurrent retirement liabilities in half from $1,134 million to $545 million (Note I).

ROIC vs. WACC & Economic Value Creation: Trailing ROIC is 13.22% and ROE is 18.01% against an estimated ~8.5% WACC [13]. That gives GD roughly +470 basis points of positive economic spread above its cost of capital [13]. Crucially, GD achieves this spread with modest leverage (0.33x Debt/Equity) and strong cash backing rather than financial engineering [11][13].

Dividend Coverage & Capital Return Sustainability: GD carries a 38.83% earnings payout ratio ($6.27 TTM dividend) and 6.40% 5-year annual dividend growth [11][13]. Across 9M 2026, GD generated $4,827 million in FCF, up from $3,007 million in 9M 2025. That cash easily covered $1,263 million in cash dividends (~3.8x 9M FCF coverage), $1,000 million in note repayments, and $500 million in pension funding. GD also spent $604 million on share repurchases, retiring 1.7 million shares and leaving 5.1 million shares (1.9%) authorized at October 4, 2026 (Note K, Exhibit G). Diluted shares fell from ~305 million in FY2016 to ~270.2 million basic and 273.8 million diluted in Q3 2026 [9][11][13].

book_paragraphs: Now let's put on our forensic accountant hat and examine ten years of General Dynamics' financial statements from 2016 through 2025. What jumps out first is the sheer steadiness of the compounding engine. Revenue grew from $30.56 billion in 2016 to $52.55 billion in 2025, while diluted EPS rose from $9.52 to $15.45—and hit $17.01 trailing twelve months through Q3 2026. Even during the 2020 pandemic shock, operating income only dipped modestly from $4.57 billion to $4.13 billion before marching higher.

Second, look at the balance sheet discipline. In 2018, General Dynamics borrowed heavily to buy CSRA, pushing long-term debt from $4.0 billion to $11.4 billion. Over the next seven years, management systematically paid that debt down to $7.01 billion by December 31, 2025—with $1.01 billion in current maturities and $2.33 billion in cash sitting against $25.62 billion in shareholders' equity. That deliberate deleveraging is the real reason ROE stepped down from ~26% in 2018–2019 to ~18% today: the denominator grew healthier while net debt shrank to less than one turn of EBITDA. Meanwhile, ROIC sits at 13.22%, clearing an estimated 7.5% to 8.0% cost of capital by more than 500 basis points.

Where should a skeptical forensic accountant poke? Right into working capital and goodwill. At October 4, 2026, General Dynamics carried $8,906 million in net unbilled receivables ($47,157 million unbilled revenue less $38,251 million progress billings, up from $8,380 million at year-end 2025) and $9,124 million in inventories, mostly Gulfstream jets in production. Combined, unbilled receivables and inventories sit near $18.0 billion—though customer advances and deposits of $13,705 million ($11,083 million current plus $2,622 million noncurrent) finance the vast majority of that work-in-process.

In the Q3 2026 Form 10-Q footnotes, we find two critical updates on receivables quality. First, $1.2 billion of net unbilled receivables sits on that single large international tracked-vehicle contract in Combat Systems (down slightly from $1.3 billion at year-end 2025), and Note B explicitly cautions that actual variable consideration realized could fall below current estimates and materially impact results. Second, correcting an earlier secondary summary, neither the FY2025 Form 10-K nor the Q3 2026 Form 10-Q shows an active MARPA receivable-factoring program—meaning the $5,745 million of 9M 2026 operating cash flow ($4,827 million FCF; 139% Q3 CFO conversion) comes cleanly from organic operations and milestone collections.

Take a step back and synthesize all six chapters of our price-blind audit. General Dynamics passes our business-quality screen as a durable compounder: it owns irreplaceable nuclear submarine infrastructure, a high-margin Gulfstream duopoly, and a fortress balance sheet, with KPI health rated PASS_WITH_WATCH only because we want to see Marine Systems margins climb back above 8.5% and G400 certification cross the finish line.

Our footnote audit also uncovered four balance-sheet items that headline debt metrics overlook. First, GD carries $20,849 million in goodwill—76.4% of shareholders' equity—with $14,515 million sitting in Technologies (net of $1.8 billion in prior impairment losses) and last quantitatively tested in Q4 2022 with ~25% headroom. Second, while total debt fell to $7,016 million against $4,388 million in cash ($2,628 million net debt) after repaying $1,000 million of 2026 notes, $2,250 million of fixed-rate notes mature between April 2027 and May 2028 ($750 million in April 2027, $500 million in November 2027, and $1,000 million in May 2028) alongside a $4 billion credit facility expiring March 2027. Third, GD carries $2,014 million in lease liabilities ($334 million current, $1,680 million noncurrent). Fourth, management deployed $500 million in Q3 2026 to fund qualified pension plans (whose underfunded plans carried an $11,540 million PBO vs. $10,606 million assets at year-end 2025), cutting noncurrent retirement liabilities in half from $1,134 million to $545 million.

That conservative 0.33x debt-to-equity ratio gives General Dynamics enormous strategic flexibility. It can fund $1.2 billion to $1.5 billion in annual capital expenditures for submarine dry docks and Savannah hangars, pay a growing $6.27-per-share dividend (only a 38.8% payout ratio), retire maturing notes in cash, and still buy back shares whenever the stock dips below intrinsic value. On earnings quality, 122% CFO-to-net-income conversion in FY2025 and 139% in Q3 2026 confirm that GD's profits are real cash, not accrual accounting.

When you put all ten years of financial statements side by side, the single most important number on the page is that 13.22% return on invested capital against an 8.5% cost of capital. That +470-basis-point spread tells you that every dollar General Dynamics reinvests into submarine dry docks, Gulfstream completion hangars, and Combat Systems tooling creates genuine economic value.

Even better, management is not juicing that return with reckless debt. With a 0.33x debt-to-equity ratio, 122% FY2025 operating cash flow conversion, and $500 million of debt retired in Q3 2026 alone, the balance sheet is built to weather both defense-budget squabbles and commercial aviation slowdowns.

For long-term investors, that 38.83% payout ratio is quietly one of the most attractive features in the entire 10-year ledger. General Dynamics has grown its dividend at roughly 6.4% annually over the past five years without ever stretching its balance sheet. Because free cash flow covers the dividend more than two-and-a-half times over, the company can keep raising its payout through recessions while simultaneously paying down debt and shrinking the share count.

In short, the 10-year forensic ledger confirms that General Dynamics' earnings are backed by real cash, conservative leverage, and a +470-basis-point ROIC spread over its cost of capital—precisely the profile we look for in a long-term compounder.

This combination of 122% free cash flow conversion, 0.33x debt-to-equity, and a 38.8% dividend payout ratio gives General Dynamics one of the most durable balance sheets in the entire S&P 500 industrials sector.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Ten-year forensics confirm that General Dynamics is a high-quality industrial compounder, not an accounting mirage. Free cash flow averaged ~$3.4 billion per year from 2020 to 2025 even while funding $1 billion/year in capex, and 122%–139% CFO conversion proves earnings are backed by real cash.
